extracted.intended_audience: general Fox News readers interested in media and politics
extracted.subtask_description: A news article reporting on Bari Weiss's resignation from the New York Times and commentary alleging censorship and ideological bias at the paper; presents quotes from critics and the paper's response. Useful for evaluating arguments about journalism ethics, newsroom culture, and editorial decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outright censorship / restricting diversity of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: “What this journalist has done is not just to indict, but to convict The New York Times of outright censorship.” / “There is, indeed, a backhanded sort of censorship going on here.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics argue the Times is restricting the flow of ideas and narrowing debate; Weiss says the paper 'is choosing to restrict the flow of ideas and dialogue.' This criterion is used to evaluate whether a news outlet suppresses dissenting viewpoints or narrows public discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics in journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: “If it doesn’t send shockwaves through the world of journalism, it’s because the world of journalism no longer has ethics.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bozell’s remark treats adherence to ethical standards as a core measure of journalistic quality; failure to uphold ethics (e.g., fairness, independence) is presented as a central indictment of the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid letting social media dictate news selection
rubrics_metrics.description: “Twitter that is leading the news today, that reporters are looking at their Twitter feeds and determining what is or isn’t news based on that silly contraption.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bozell and others argue it’s problematic when reporters and editors prioritize Twitter reactions over independent editorial judgment; examples cited include staff backlash over the Tom Cotton op-ed and subsequent editorial changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not tailoring stories to satisfy the narrowest audience
rubrics_metrics.description: “Stories are chosen and told in a way to satisfy the narrowest of audiences.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weiss’s claim implies a failing where stories are selected to placate specific online or niche groups rather than broader public interest; evaluators should look for evidence of audience-targeted storytelling that narrows coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value intellectual curiosity (don’t treat it as a liability)
rubrics_metrics.description: “'Intellectual curiosity' is a liability at the Times.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece presents intellectual curiosity as a positive journalistic trait that should be encouraged; treating curiosity as a liability signals a problematic editorial culture that discourages questioning and exploration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid crusaderism/advocacy that narrows debate
rubrics_metrics.description: “It's unmistakable crusaderism for left-of-center causes reflects a narrowing of debate in the public sphere.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: McCall frames advocacy or crusader journalism (especially for a partisan cause) as a defect because it reduces the range of viewpoints and harms public deliberation; assessing whether reporting is advocacy vs. balanced reporting is the test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vetting and verifying claims
rubrics_metrics.description: “Weiss’ claims need to be vetted and verified.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when allegations align with observed coverage, critics note that claims should be checked; this criterion emphasizes fact-checking and corroboration of internal allegations before accepting them as true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish voices and viewpoints across the political spectrum
rubrics_metrics.description: “We appreciate the many contributions that Bari made... I’m personally committed to ensuring that The Times continues to publish voices, experiences and viewpoints from across the political spectrum in the Opinion report.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial commitment to ideological diversity in opinion pages is offered as a corrective or standard; evaluators should check whether a publication's opinion content represents a range of political perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use agenda-setting responsibility wisely
rubrics_metrics.description: “The New York Times is perhaps the key agenda-setter for the rest of the news industry in the United States, and that is a serious responsibility.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because major outlets influence the broader media agenda, this criterion assesses whether an outlet exercises that influence responsibly — e.g., by fostering diverse debate and avoiding narrowing the national conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid intolerant newsroom culture that silences dissent
rubrics_metrics.description: “The vicious social justice warfare culture has moved from campus to newsrooms, and there is no place for old-fashioned liberals like Weiss.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jacobson’s comment frames an intolerant internal culture as a failing; evaluators should look for evidence that dissenting colleagues are bullied, marginalized, or driven out, which would indicate a problematic workplace affecting editorial outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not placate or capitulate to online mobs
rubrics_metrics.description: “Twitter hated what Senator Cotton had to say, and therefore, The New York Times genuflected... placating the online mob that wishes to silence its political opponents.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Tom Cotton op-ed episode is cited as an example: the newspaper’s correction/ mea culpa and Editorial Page Editor resignation are presented as evidence of capitulation. This criterion flags instances where editorial decisions appear driven by online backlash rather than editorial standards.
